landmarks.name: Woodmen Tower (Woodmen of the World HQ)
landmarks.appearance: 30-story International Style rectangular slab tower with straight lines and little decoration. One source says it is faced in red granite with carved beehive ornament. Flat roof. Tallest building in Nebraska 1969-2002, so it should be the tallest thing on the 1993 skyline.
landmarks.notes: Built 1966-69 by Leo A. Daly and Kiewit; opened April 1969. It stands on the site of the old City Hall and the Bee Building (both demolished 1966). Now called WoodmenLife Tower; in 1993 it was the Woodmen Tower.

landmarks.name: First National Center (1971 First National Bank of Omaha tower)
landmarks.appearance: 22-story Modern Movement tower: a geometric limestone colonnade base with a glass tower that seems to float above it. Roof at 295 ft, with a rooftop antenna mast rising to 383 ft. Second-tallest building in 1993.
landmarks.notes: Completed 1971. First National's HQ until its 45-story tower across Dodge opened in 2002.

landmarks.name: Northwestern Bell / US WEST headquarters (now the Omaha World-Herald Building)
landmarks.appearance: Modern office tower: a 12-story main block, a central slice rising 2 more floors, and 16 floors in total (Skyscraper Center gives 80 m / ~262 ft). Exterior materials not confirmed; model it as a boxy late-1970s corporate tower with a stepped center section.
landmarks.notes: Completed 1980-81 as the new Northwestern Bell HQ. Northwestern Bell was part of US WEST from 1984 to 1999, so in 1993 it was the phone company's building. It later became the Qwest building, and the World-Herald bought it in 2006. It was NOT the World-Herald building in 1993.

landmarks.name: Northwestern Bell Telephone Co. Regional HQ (older building; now the AT&T Building)
landmarks.appearance: 16-story simple rectangular modernist block with granite and brick veneers and rows of aluminum-framed windows. It began as a 12-story building (1957) and got a matching addition in 1962. On the block bounded by Dodge, Douglas, 19th and 20th.
landmarks.notes: Leo A. Daly design. Northwestern Bell's HQ until 1981; it stayed a phone-company building afterward.

landmarks.name: Union Pacific Headquarters (1911 building)
landmarks.nearestIntersection: 14th & Dodge (block bounded by 14th, 15th, Dodge and Capitol Ave)
landmarks.appearance: Early-1900s masonry office block that filled most of a city block, with an annex added in 1971. Exact story count was not found; model it as a mid-rise (roughly 10-12 stories, estimated) brown or tan masonry block.
landmarks.notes: UP's HQ from 1911 to 2004. This is the UP building of 1993. It was torn down in the mid-2000s (sources say 2006-2008). The site sat empty for years; a planned 32-story condo tower was never built.

landmarks.name: Omaha World-Herald Building (World-Herald Square)
landmarks.appearance: Late-1940s low- to mid-rise newspaper plant and office block with a distinctive rounded-corner main entrance. It held both the newsroom and the printing presses. Height was not found; model it as a wide 4-6 story block (estimate).
landmarks.notes: Completed 1948. It was the World-Herald's HQ and press plant from 1948 to 2006, so this is the 1993 World-Herald building. Demolition began in March 2008; the curved entrance was kept as a gateway to a green space.

landmarks.name: Douglas County Courthouse
landmarks.appearance: French Renaissance Revival civic building: Bedford limestone walls on a granite base, arcaded front entrance, engaged Corinthian columns and piers, and pediments on the projecting wings. Five stories exposed on the north side and six on the south. An octagonal dome sits at the center of the roof. Set back from Farnam. Pale gray-buff stone. Roughly 90-110 ft to the dome top (estimate).
landmarks.notes: Built 1909-1912 by John Latenser Sr. On the National Register since 1979.

landmarks.name: Omaha-Douglas Civic Center (Omaha City Hall)
landmarks.appearance: 12-story rectangular steel, glass and concrete modernist office block on landscaped grounds just west of the courthouse. Plain and functional, with no ornament. About 150-170 ft (estimate).
landmarks.notes: Built 1972-74 by Leo A. Daly and Hawkins Construction. Holds city and county offices and county courtrooms. Some sources give conflicting dates; 1972-74 is the construction date.

landmarks.name: Omaha Civic Auditorium
landmarks.appearance: 1954 arena complex with a large arched roof over the main arena (9,300 seats for sports, 10,960 for concerts), plus an attached Music Hall (about 2,450 seats) and an exhibit hall (43,400 sq ft). Model it as a wide, low mass with a barrel-vault roof. Materials not confirmed.
landmarks.notes: Leo A. Daly and Kiewit. Home of Creighton men's basketball from 1960 to 2003, so Creighton played here in 1993. Closed June 2014 and demolished 2016.

landmarks.name: Orpheum Theater
landmarks.appearance: 1927 Italianate movie and vaudeville palace entered from 16th St, with about 2,600 seats. In 1993 it had the steel-letter marquee added in the 1973-75 renovation (the digital marquee came much later). It is attached to the 16-story City National Bank Building at the corner.
landmarks.notes: Bought by Ak-Sar-Ben in 1972 and reopened in 1975 as a performing arts hall for the symphony, opera and ballet. Further renovations in 1996, 2002 and 2017 all came after 1993.

landmarks.name: City National Bank Building (Orpheum Tower)
landmarks.appearance: 16-story early skyscraper (1910), Omaha's tallest when it was built. Classic tripartite masonry tower over the Orpheum.
landmarks.notes: Pair it with the Orpheum as one model group.

landmarks.name: Central Park Plaza
landmarks.appearance: Two 15-story red-brick office towers set in a 'V' formation and joined by a low 2-story connector. It faces the west end of the Central Park (Gene Leahy) Mall.

landmarks.name: 1200 Landmark Center
landmarks.appearance: 15-story postmodern office tower with a distinctive crown of four rooftop peaks (gables).
landmarks.notes: Completed 1990, so it was new in 1993. The exact address and intersection were not confirmed; it sits by the north side of the mall near 13th.

landmarks.name: Brandeis Building
landmarks.appearance: 10-story 1906 former department store block with a masonry facade. After 1981 it held offices, retail and a food court, with 2 atriums and a skywalk to Parkfair Mall.
landmarks.notes: The Brandeis store closed in 1980, so in 1993 it was an office and retail conversion, not a department store.

landmarks.name: Old Market warehouse district
landmarks.appearance: Dense blocks of red-brick 19th- and early-20th-century wholesale warehouses, mostly 3-7 stories. Brick-paved streets from about 1900, some cobblestone and asphalt, covered sidewalks (canopies) along parts of the blocks, and horse-drawn carriages. Key spots: the Old Market Passageway (a roofed brick alley at the NE corner of 11th & Howard, opened 1977), M's Pub building (11th & Howard), French Cafe (1017 Howard), Spaghetti Works.
landmarks.notes: The Mercer family started converting the buildings in the 1960s-70s; the district was nominated to the National Register in 1979. The French Cafe was open 1969-2012, so it existed in 1993.

landmarks.name: Central Park Mall / Gene Leahy Mall and lagoon
landmarks.address: Between Farnam and Douglas, 10th to 14th in 1993
landmarks.appearance: Sunken linear park with a long lagoon that split the park into north and south halves. Waterfalls, fountains, an elevated pedestrian walkway, big 'jumbo' metal playground slides near 11th & Farnam, and swans. Grass banks slope down to the water; bridges cross the lagoon.
landmarks.notes: Lawrence Halprin design (1974); first block opened June 1977. Renamed Gene Leahy Mall in 1992, so in 1993 both names were in use. The 8th-10th St section was not finished until 1995, so end it around 10th St for 1993. The 2019-2022 redesign must NOT appear.

landmarks.name: W. Dale Clark Library (Omaha Public Library main branch)
landmarks.appearance: Late-1970s modernist block clad in Bedford limestone (pale buff), 124,500 sq ft, a few stories tall. Model it as a low, heavy stone-clad box.
landmarks.notes: Opened March 1977 (John Latenser & Sons). Closed 2022 and later demolished for the Mutual of Omaha tower.

landmarks.name: Joslyn Art Museum
landmarks.appearance: Monumental 1931 Art Deco temple-like block clad in Georgia Pink marble (pinkish stone), with a marble retaining wall. Low and wide (about 2-3 stories equivalent). In summer 1993 there was only the original building; the glass-atrium Scott Pavilion was under construction or not yet built.
landmarks.notes: Designed by John and Alan McDonald. The Norman Foster Scott Pavilion was completed in 1994, so leave it out or show a construction site. The Snohetta wing is much later.

landmarks.name: Omaha Central High School
landmarks.appearance: Hollow-square French Renaissance Revival school, 250 x 225 ft: 3 stories over a raised basement around a central courtyard. Rusticated stone on the basement and first floor, smooth ashlar above, Bedford limestone trim. The courtyard has a translucent dome roof (added 1981-82). It sits on a hill: the old Territorial Capitol site.
landmarks.notes: Built 1900-1912 by John Latenser Sr. On the National Register since 1979.

landmarks.name: Creighton University campus
landmarks.appearance: Campus north of I-480 and east of the North Freeway, centered on St. John's Church: an 1888 English Gothic Revival church in Warrensburg sandstone with Bedford stone trim and add-on towers. Mostly 1960s modernist buildings around it. The tallest on the main campus were Kiewit Hall (9-story dorm, 1966) and the similar-sized Swanson Hall (1964). Also Deglman Hall, Gallagher Hall and the Criss medical complex.
landmarks.notes: Kiewit Hall was demolished in 2024, so it existed in 1993. Creighton basketball played downtown at the Civic Auditorium.

landmarks.name: Mutual of Omaha HQ
landmarks.appearance: 14-story midtown office tower (1970 addition to a 1940 building). A large glass dome skylight (1979) sits at ground level on the SW corner of 33rd & Dodge, above 3 underground floors and tunnels.
landmarks.notes: The new 677-ft downtown Mutual tower is from 2026; do not use it.

landmarks.name: Kiewit Plaza (Berkshire Hathaway HQ)
landmarks.appearance: 15-story modernist office slab (1960-61).
landmarks.notes: Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway has been headquartered here since 1962. It was renamed Blackstone Plaza in 2019; in 1993 it was Kiewit Plaza.

landmarks.name: Blackstone Hotel / Blackstone Center
landmarks.appearance: 8-story Second Renaissance Revival building: steel frame clad in brick with a terracotta cornice (about 100 ft, estimate).
landmarks.notes: Opened 1916; closed as a hotel in 1976. Renovated in 1984 into offices called Blackstone Center, so in 1993 it was an office building. It reopened as a hotel much later.

landmarks.name: Omaha Star newspaper building
landmarks.appearance: One-story rectangular brown-brick commercial building with a flat roof and crenellated parapet. Decorative brick piers on limestone bases between recessed windows, a corner entrance under a metal awning, red-and-white scalloped metal awnings over the windows, and chain-link over the window glass.
landmarks.notes: Home of the Omaha Star since July 1938. Mildred Brown lived in the back apartment until her death in 1989. Listed on the National Register 2007-08.

landmarks.name: Jewell Building (Dreamland Ballroom)
landmarks.appearance: Two-story brick building in a vernacular Georgian Revival style, with shops on the ground floor and the ballroom hall on the second floor.
landmarks.notes: Built 1923. The Dreamland Ballroom closed in 1975. The Omaha Economic Development Council restored the exterior and renovated the interior in 1985, so it looked restored in 1993. The Great Plains Black History Museum moved in only in 2017.

landmarks.name: Fair Deal Cafe
landmarks.appearance: Small storefront diner. By 1995 it was the only building left standing on its block, so model it with vacant lots around it.
landmarks.notes: Open 1954-2003; known as the 'Black City Hall' of North Omaha.

landmarks.name: Skeet's Ribs & Chicken
landmarks.appearance: Small 1950s single-story barbecue restaurant building.
landmarks.notes: Built around 1955. Run by David Deal from 1978 until 2019, so it was operating in 1993.

landmarks.name: Former Safeway / Omaha Small Business Network building
landmarks.appearance: 1960s single-story supermarket box reused as offices.
landmarks.notes: Built 1963 and targeted in the 1967-68 riots; the store closed in 1968. It reopened in 1983 as the Omaha Small Business Network's Business Technology Center.

landmarks.name: Peterson's Bakery building (later Love's Jazz & Art Center)
landmarks.appearance: Early-20th-century brick commercial storefront at the 24th & Lake corner (it appears in 1969 riot photos).
landmarks.notes: What occupied it in 1993 was not confirmed; it became Love's Jazz & Art Center later.

landmarks.name: Great Plains Black History Museum (Webster Telephone Exchange Building)
landmarks.appearance: 1906 brick telephone exchange building (small, 2-3 stories, estimate).
landmarks.notes: Bertha Calloway opened the museum here on Feb 8, 1976. It closed in 2004 and reopened at 2221 N 24th in 2017, so in 1993 it was at 2213 Lake St.

landmarks.name: Malcolm X birthsite
landmarks.appearance: Mostly an empty grassy lot. The Little family house was demolished in 1965; the official Nebraska State Historical Society marker was dedicated May 19, 1987. Model a green lot with a single roadside historical marker sign.
landmarks.notes: Listed on the National Register in 1984. The Malcolm X Memorial Foundation's later plaza and educational memorial, and the current big redevelopment plans, should not appear in 1993.

landmarks.name: Kountze Park
landmarks.nearestIntersection: 19th & Pinkney (bounded by 19th, 20th, Pinkney and Pratt; Florence Blvd markers)
landmarks.appearance: Neighborhood block park with lawns, trees, playground, courts and a pavilion. Surrounded by Victorian houses of the Kountze Place neighborhood.
landmarks.notes: Site of the 1898 Trans-Mississippi Exposition. It was once also called Malcolm X Park. The exact 1993 facilities were not confirmed (the water park may be later).

landmarks.name: Bemis Park
landmarks.appearance: A 200-ft-wide strip of park running from 33rd to 36th just north of Cuming, mostly a deep, narrow wooded ravine. It is surrounded by curving streets that follow the terrain, unlike Omaha's grid, with Queen Anne, Arts & Crafts and Neo-Classical homes.
landmarks.notes: The Bemis Park district (Cuming to Hawthorne, 33rd to 40th) became an Omaha Landmark district in 1983.

landmarks.name: Miller Park
landmarks.nearestIntersection: 30th & Redick (bounded by Redick, Kansas Ave, 24th and 30th)
landmarks.appearance: Large Victorian-era park with a lake (fed by Minne Lusa Creek), a golf course (opened 1916) and the 1908 pavilion: 3 stories with a wrap-around covered porch, brick pillars, wood railings, and two chateau-like A-frame end sections joined by a middle section.
landmarks.notes: Added to the city in 1891. The golf course was renamed for Steve Hogan in 2009; in 1993 it was the Miller Park course.

landmarks.name: Logan Fontenelle Homes (housing project)
landmarks.appearance: PWA-era project originally of 29 one- and two-story brick buildings (284 apartments), laid out in rows. In summer 1993 it was partly demolished: some rows boarded up or standing, others cleared lots.
landmarks.notes: Opened 1937-38 (Everett S. Dodds). The OHA began demolition in 1991 and finished around 1995-96, so it was partial in 1993. The mixed-income Conestoga neighborhood came afterward.

landmarks.name: Pleasantview Homes (housing project)
landmarks.address: Both sides of N 30th St, Burdette south to Parker
landmarks.appearance: Barracks-style layout on 14 acres: about 16 one- and two-story brick buildings (184 units in the 2-story blocks), plus the 6-story, 51-unit Pleasantview Towers. Described as isolated and maze-like.
landmarks.notes: Leo A. Daly design (1953). Sources give different end dates (1996, 2008, 2009), but all agree it stood in 1993. The Highlander neighborhood later replaced it.

landmarks.name: Hilltop Homes (housing project)
landmarks.appearance: Early-1950s public housing on a 14-acre hillside site. Building form not confirmed; model it like the neighboring 1950s brick barracks-style blocks.
landmarks.notes: Built 1952 and demolished 1995, so it was standing in 1993. Salem Baptist Church and a Walgreens are on the site now and must not appear.

landmarks.name: Spencer Homes (housing project)
landmarks.appearance: Barracks-style two-story public housing blocks. Split in two by the North Freeway: 57 units were removed in 1981 and replaced with newer units in 1983.
landmarks.notes: Opened June 1952 (Leo A. Daly) with 165 units. Demolished 2022; Kennedy Square redevelopment followed.

landmarks.name: North Freeway (US-75) and Sorensen Parkway
landmarks.appearance: Sunken or elevated urban freeway cutting north through North Omaha from I-480 past Lake St to Sorensen Pkwy and the Storz Expressway.
landmarks.notes: The final section north of Lake St opened Nov 15, 1988; Sorensen Pkwy and Storz Expressway opened 1989. It was complete in 1993.

landmarks.name: Time Out Foods
landmarks.appearance: Small fast-food fried-chicken restaurant building.
landmarks.notes: Opened Aug 4, 1969. Whether it was operating in 1993 was not confirmed; it has closed and reopened over the years.

landmarks.name: Rosenblatt Stadium
landmarks.nearestIntersection: 13th & Deer Park Blvd (site ran along Deer Park Blvd between 10th and 13th)
landmarks.appearance: Hilltop baseball stadium with a grandstand under a peaked roof, painted 'Rosenblatt blue', and red, yellow and blue seats. It overlooks the zoo across the street. It had been expanding through the 1980s-90s (over $20M of work 1979-1999); final capacity was 23,145.
landmarks.notes: Opened 1948 as Municipal Stadium. Home of the College World Series 1950-2010 and of the Omaha Royals (AAA) in 1993. Demolished after 2010.

landmarks.name: Henry Doorly Zoo
landmarks.address: 3701 S 10th St (address from general knowledge; not confirmed by these sources)
landmarks.appearance: Zoo grounds next to Rosenblatt. The main 1993 icon is the Lied Jungle: an 80-ft-tall, 1.5-acre building with a translucent roof held up by steel columns disguised as trees.
landmarks.notes: The Lied Jungle opened April 4, 1992. The old aquarium closed in 1993 while the new Scott Aquarium was built (opened 1995). The Desert Dome (2002) and Kingdoms of the Night (2003) must be left out.

landmarks.name: Livestock Exchange Building and Union Stockyards
landmarks.address: 4920 S 30th St (also given as 2900 O Plaza)
landmarks.appearance: 11-story H-shaped tower: steel frame in concrete with dark red brick curtain walls in a decorative pattern, Romanesque / Northern Italian Renaissance Revival, with an arched entry portico and plaza. It towered over about 200 acres of wooden livestock pens and barns. About 150 ft (estimate).
landmarks.notes: Opened May 1926 (George Prinz; built by Kiewit). The stockyards were still operating in 1993 but in decline: the last big packing house closed in 1976 and the yards closed in 1999. The pens are parking lots today.

landmarks.name: Vinton Street grain elevator
landmarks.appearance: Huge slip-formed concrete terminal elevator: rows of tubular silos two blocks long (Vinton south to Valley St) with a tall concrete headhouse. Once Omaha's largest grain elevator.
landmarks.notes: Completed 1950 by Tillotson Construction. Whether it was running in 1993 was not confirmed; it is abandoned now. Its silhouette is clearly visible from I-80.

landmarks.name: Ak-Sar-Ben racetrack and Coliseum
landmarks.appearance: Thoroughbred horse track with an oval, a large grandstand (11,500) and the 1929 Coliseum arena (7,200) next to it. Large parking lots. It is in central/west Omaha, outside the core districts.
landmarks.notes: Track opened 1919-20 and closed Aug 7, 1995, so racing was still on in summer 1993. The Coliseum was home to the Omaha Racers (CBA) 1989-97. Everything was demolished in 2005; Aksarben Village came later.

landmarks.name: Eppley Airfield
landmarks.nearestIntersection: Abbott Dr (East Omaha, next to Carter Lake, IA)
landmarks.appearance: Mid-size airport on the west bank of the Missouri NE of downtown: a 1961 terminal, Concourse B (1970, remodeled 1986), Concourse A (1986) and a 1975 control tower.
landmarks.notes: The Carter Lake, Iowa enclave sits right next to it. Later terminal modernizations should not appear.

landmarks.name: I-480 Missouri River bridge (Grenville Dodge Memorial Bridge)
landmarks.nearestIntersection: I-480 east of downtown (Douglas St corridor)
landmarks.appearance: Eight-lane steel plate-girder highway bridge, 1,687 ft long, low and flat (no truss).
landmarks.notes: Built 1965-66 to replace the Ak-Sar-Ben (Douglas St) truss bridge; opened Nov 12, 1966.

landmarks.name: Union Pacific Missouri River Bridge
landmarks.nearestIntersection: North of downtown riverfront (exact street not confirmed)
landmarks.appearance: Double-track railroad through-truss bridge, 1,750 ft long, 62 ft above the river, on piers reused from the 1880s bridge.
landmarks.notes: Opened Dec 20, 1916, at the site of the first 1872 transcontinental crossing.

landmarks.name: I-80 Missouri River bridge
landmarks.appearance: Interstate highway girder bridge.
landmarks.notes: Opened Dec 15, 1972.

landmarks.name: South Omaha Veterans Memorial Bridge (old truss)
landmarks.appearance: Long, narrow continuous Warren through-truss steel bridge, 4,378 ft long, with only a 22.5-ft roadway.
landmarks.notes: Opened Jan 18, 1936. Closed Sept 2009 and replaced in 2010; the 1993 map needs the old truss.

landmarks.name: Mormon Bridge (I-680)
landmarks.appearance: Twin cantilevered Warren through-truss bridges (1952 span plus a second span added in the 1970s).
landmarks.notes: The tolls ended in 1979 when it joined the Interstate system.

landmarks.name: Heartland of America Park and ConAgra campus
landmarks.appearance: 31-acre park with an artificial lake between I-80 and the river. It has a computerized fountain shooting water 300 ft high with night lights. ConAgra's low-rise suburban-style HQ campus sits at the south end of the lake.
landmarks.notes: The park opened Sept 1990 and the ConAgra HQ was completed around 1990-92. Both are on the site of Jobbers Canyon, which was demolished 1988-89.

landmarks.name: ASARCO lead refinery
landmarks.appearance: Heavy industrial riverfront plant (sheds, stacks, rail sidings). No detailed physical description was found.
landmarks.notes: Ran for more than 100 years and closed in 1997; demolished by late 1999. The site became Lewis & Clark Landing around 2001. It should be an active smelter on the 1993 riverfront.

landmarks.name: Union Station (Western Heritage Museum)
landmarks.appearance: 1931 Midwestern Art Deco railroad station (Gilbert Stanley Underwood; built by Kiewit), with tall vertical window bays and cream stone. It is on the bluff above the rail yards.
landmarks.notes: Passenger service ended in 1971. It was the Western Heritage Museum from 1975 to 1997 (later the Durham Museum), so in 1993 it was the Western Heritage Museum.

landmarks.name: Burlington Station
landmarks.appearance: 1898 Thomas R. Kimball station (heavily remodeled), with a large track canopy. Next to the rail yards and Little Italy.
landmarks.notes: Amtrak left in 1974. It was most likely vacant in 1993 (not confirmed) and became the KETV studio much later.

landmarks.name: Peony Park
landmarks.appearance: 35-acre amusement park: a 4.5-acre pool with a sand beach and waterslide, a ballroom billed as '1 acre under one roof', an open-air dance floor, a roller coaster, Ferris wheel, carousel, Wave Swinger, Tilt-A-Whirl, bumper cars and a train.
landmarks.notes: Open 1919 to March 31, 1994, so summer 1993 was one of its last seasons. The owners filed for bankruptcy in 1991. It is in west-central Omaha.

landmarks.name: Council Bluffs skyline and bluffs (across the river)
landmarks.appearance: Low skyline. The biggest downtown building is the 8-story Hotel Chieftain (1927); the historic Bennett Building is only 86 ft. Behind the town rise the steep Loess Hills bluffs, with the 1935 Lewis & Clark Monument (stone markers and an overlook) at Rainbow Point. Bluffs Run Greyhound Park (1986) is on the flats. UP rail yards and the transfer yard are on the Iowa side.
landmarks.notes: In 1993 there were NO casinos: slots came to Bluffs Run in March 1995 and the riverboat casinos (Ameristar, Harveys) in 1996. The Mid-America Center came in 2002.

notYetBuiltIn1993: First National Bank Tower (45 stories, 634 ft, 1601 Dodge St), completed 2002. The 1993 skyline peak is the Woodmen Tower.
Union Pacific Center (1400 Douglas St, 19 stories, 317 ft), opened June 2004. In 1993 UP was in its 1911 HQ at 14th & Dodge.
Qwest Center Omaha (now CHI Health Center), opened Sept 20, 2003. In 1993 big events used the Civic Auditorium and the Ak-Sar-Ben Coliseum.
Holland Performing Arts Center (13th & Douglas), opened Oct 2005.
Bob Kerrey Pedestrian Bridge (cable-stayed), opened Sept 28, 2008.
TD Ameritrade Park / Charles Schwab Field (downtown), opened 2011. In 1993 the College World Series was at Rosenblatt.
Omaha World-Herald Freedom Center printing plant (14th & Capitol), opened Aug 2001.
The World-Herald in the 1314 Douglas building: it moved there only in 2006. In 1993 it was at World-Herald Square, 1334 Dodge.
Joslyn Art Museum Scott Pavilion (Norman Foster), completed 1994, and the later Snohetta wing.
Henry Doorly Zoo Scott Aquarium (1995), Desert Dome (2002) and Kingdoms of the Night (2003).
Gene Leahy Mall's 8th-10th St section (finished 1995) and the 2019-2022 RiverFront redesign.
Lewis & Clark Landing and the Storz Brewing riverfront site, on the ASARCO smelter site (ASARCO closed 1997; site donated about 2001).
Council Bluffs casinos: Bluffs Run slots (March 1995), Ameristar riverboat (Jan 1996), Harveys riverboat (1996, later Harrah's).
Mid-America Center, Council Bluffs (Oct 2002).
New South Omaha Veterans Memorial Bridge (2010). The 1936 truss was still in use in 1993.
Mutual of Omaha Headquarters Tower downtown (677 ft, topped out 2025, done in 2026), and the demolition of the W. Dale Clark Library for it.
Aksarben Village, UNO dorms and Baxter Arena on the Ak-Sar-Ben site (after the 2005 demolition).
Highlander neighborhood (on the Pleasantview/Hilltop site), Salem Baptist Church and Walgreens at 30th & Lake, and Kennedy Square (the Spencer Homes replacement).
Conestoga mixed-income neighborhood replacing Logan Fontenelle (after the 1991-95 demolition).
Great Plains Black History Museum at 2221 N 24th (moved there in 2017). In 1993 it was at 2213 Lake St.
The Malcolm X birthsite plaza and educational memorial (later). In 1993 there was just a lot with the 1987 state marker.
The 'Blackstone Plaza' name for Kiewit Plaza (2019) and the 'WoodmenLife Tower' name. Use 'Kiewit Plaza' and 'Woodmen Tower'.
demolishedBefore1993: Old City Hall ('Red Castle', 1890) and the Bee Building (1888) at 17th & Farnam, both demolished 1966 (the Woodmen Tower site)
Old Post Office at 16th & Dodge (1898), demolished 1966
Ak-Sar-Ben (Douglas Street) Bridge, an 1888 Whipple truss, demolished 1968 except a small west pier
Woodmen of the World Building (1912), demolished Dec 18, 1977
Hotel Fontenelle (18th & Douglas, 1915 Gothic Revival, 16 stories above ground), empty from 1971 and demolished 1983
Jobbers Canyon Historic District (six blocks of 7-8 story red-brick warehouses east of the Old Market), demolished 1988-89 for ConAgra and Heartland of America Park
Many North 24th St blocks between Clark and Lake, bulldozed after the 1966-69 riots and left as vacant lots
57 Spencer Homes units, demolished in 1981 for the North Freeway
Logan Fontenelle Homes, partly: demolition began in 1991 and the complex was not fully gone until about 1995

Closed but still standing in 1993: Brandeis department store (closed 1980, converted to offices), Dreamland Ballroom (closed 1975; building restored 1985), Safeway at 24th & Lake (closed 1968; reused 1983), Blackstone Hotel (closed 1976; Blackstone Center offices from 1984), Union Station passenger service (ended 1971), Burlington Station (Amtrak left 1974), and the last major South Omaha packing house (closed 1976)
sources: NOTE: WebFetch was blocked for almost every domain in this environment, so all facts come from WebSearch result snippets of the pages above, not full-page reads.
